01 / Meet Will

About me.

I’m William Croteau, and I study Geographic Information Systems and Technology at Texas A&M University. I work with geographic data to understand patterns, compare places and communicate findings through maps.

My strengths are ArcGIS, cartographic design and spatial analysis. My academic work spans housing, environmental hazards, land cover and point patterns, giving me practice with both the analytical and visual sides of GIS.

What I bring to a team

Experience working with technical equipment, checking accuracy and interpreting detailed instructions, alongside a summer IT internship at LivaNova.

I’m looking to apply this combination of GIS and technical experience in a role where I can contribute and continue developing my skills.

Featured / African urbanization

Lagos: where the mapped city expanded

My component: urban growth measurement and mapping extent and flow, using footprints supplied by the project team.

Problem, approach, findings & next steps

The problem

Measure how Lagos's physical city footprint changed across observation years and locate the additions.

My contribution & workflow

My project component brings together area measurement, expansion maps, an epoch map and an exploratory corridor test. The supplied workflow uses AI-assisted Python raster overlays and ArcGIS map exports. Pair 1 supplied the classified footprints; this work does not claim independent satellite classification or field validation.

What the analysis found

The mapped city footprint increased from 497.89 km² in 2000 to 1,478.96 km² in 2024, approximately 197%. Annualized percentage growth slowed across the three reported intervals, while 2010–2018 added the most area per year. These are changes in mapped developed land, not population counts.

What I would do differently

Validate the marginal early imagery and flagged coastal classifications before drawing stronger conclusions. Separate newly developed land from existing settlements joining the city footprint, and test corridor hypotheses against dated infrastructure data.

Source: supplied Lagos Urban Growth Report and ArcGIS exports. Dates are provisional observation labels for multi-year imagery composites. The epoch map shows the 2024 footprint only; its baseline is not the complete 2000 city.
